Klyara Ltd  ·  Guildford, Surrey  ·  Written 1 September 2026 for launch on Monday 14 September 2026
Klyara is the back office for small construction firms. Bookkeeping, CIS, VAT and payroll. Construction only. Nothing else.

This plan is written to be read by Craig, by a bank, and by anyone Klyara asks for money or a partnership. It is the same document for all three, because there is nothing in it that changes depending on who is reading.

cover.title: Read this before anything else
body: Klyara has no clients. Not one. It is not yet AML supervised, so it cannot lawfully carry on bookkeeping by way of business. The ICB practice licence application goes in on Tuesday 1 September 2026 and takes about 28 days. Every revenue figure in this document is a model, built from real market prices and stated assumptions. None of it is a result. A plan that pretends otherwise is worthless, and in front of a licence application it is dangerous.

cover.cap: Four numbers, one of which is zero. Source: Klyara Financial Model.
The honest position on the day the plan was written.
Three documents, one set of numbers.

blocks.x: Klyara does the books for builders. That is the whole business.

Small construction firms have an admin problem that is specific, repeating and expensive. The Construction Industry Scheme means a return every month, on the 19th, whether or not anyone got paid. VAT in construction runs on a reverse charge that most general bookkeepers apply wrongly in at least one direction. Making Tax Digital pulls another wave of sole traders into quarterly filing in April 2027. None of it is optional and all of it is fiddly.

The gap in the market is not competence. It is that almost nobody will tell you the price. Of thirteen firms that surface for construction bookkeeping around Guildford, one publishes a full price list and it is a London firm. One local firm shows a headline number with nothing behind it. Everyone else makes you fill in a form and wait.
Klyara publishes four prices, says what is in each, and works one industry.

The four things the competitor research actually tells you

blocks.cap: The difference has to be visible in thirty seconds.

items: Almost nobody publishes a real price. One of thirteen published a full list, and it was the London firm. One local firm shows 'from as little as £35 a month' with no tiers, no transaction limits and no mention of CIS on the Guildford page.

The £35 headline needs an answer, and it is not 'we are worth more'. It is three questions: is that a 'from' price; are the CIS returns in it or billed at £15 to £30 a submission; and is the software subscription in the fee and in whose name.

'Construction specialist' is a claim, not a moat. The nearest competitor uses the same words. The honest differences are published prices, a named person who answers the phone, a Guildford address, and content that demonstrates the specialism rather than asserting it.
The nearest competitor is a national site with a town-name page. Beatable on local signals. Not beatable on domain authority. Compete where you can win.

blocks.x: Where the monthly CIS returns start, and why

blocks.cap: The single most misread line on the price list.

blocks.x: On Solo and Start, CIS is deducted from the client. Klyara records it, reconciles it to the statements the client was given, chases the ones that never arrived, and reclaims it. The client is a subcontractor, not a contractor, so there is no monthly return to file.

On Trade and Pro, the client deducts CIS from other people. That makes them a contractor and a monthly return becomes compulsory. Klyara files it on the 12th, every month, nil returns included, and issues the payment and deduction statements by the 19th.

blocks.x: Why launch low

Launching at £59 to £329 with nothing to show — no reviews, no case studies, no track record, no licence yet displayed — is defensible. Price is doing a job: it is buying the first ten clients cheaply, and the first ten clients are worth more as proof than as revenue. Raising prices before a single Google review exists would trade away the one advantage Klyara currently holds.
But three things have to be true or the low price becomes permanent.

blocks.title: The number that settles the argument
body: On twenty clients, break-even on the increase is 14.01 clients. You could lose five clients out of twenty and still be ahead — the sixth one takes you £2 a month below where you started. docs/21 targets 90% acceptance on a properly notified increase, which would be two. The downside is bounded at two clients. The upside is £14,160 a year. That asymmetry is why the founding-rate wording matters and why it costs nothing to add today.

blocks.x: Getting paid

Monthly in advance. Direct Debit preferred, standing order accepted, on the 1st, with the invoice issued on the 25th of the preceding month. Clients on Direct Debit pay on time roughly universally. Clients on bank transfer pay when they feel like it.

blocks.x: Go ICB. Cheaper, faster, and it brings a professional body, a public directory listing, discounted professional indemnity insurance, engagement letter templates and money laundering regulations guidance. The HMRC route gets you supervision on its own. There is a £500 small business reduction on the HMRC fee but it only applies under £5,000 of turnover, which will not apply.

blocks.x: What Klyara can and cannot do before the licence lands

blocks.cap: This is the law, not caution.

blocks.x: Publishing guides, running free calculators, building an email list and holding a founding-rate waitlist are all fine now. They are education, not offering. Offering or selling the service, taking a client, taking a fee or asking anyone for a review are not. Every call to action that sells is written and held, and swaps to the live version on the day supervision lands.
Two other legal points, said once

items: The homepage currently carries invented testimonials. Fake reviews and testimonials are a banned practice under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, enforceable by the CMA. They also sit in front of a licence application to a body with conduct rules on honest marketing. Remove them before anything else in this plan happens. It takes ten minutes.

Data protection. Client records are the client's. The software subscription is in the client's name precisely so that the data never becomes a lever, and a privacy notice and the client-facing paperwork are already drafted.

The current HMRC list of MTD-compatible software. HMRC maintains it and it changes.

sections.title: What happens in year two and year three

blocks.x: Two things drive years two and three, and neither of them is finding more customers.

The first is the founding-rate step-up. Every client passes their own twelve-month anniversary and moves to the standard rate, with sixty days' written notice. Across the twelve months from September 2027 the average fee moves from £138 to £197 without a single new client.

blocks.title: The choice at the end of year three
body: Three people and seventy-five clients is a good business — roughly £170,000 of revenue on a cost base that is mostly salary. Going further than that means hiring a manager, and that is a different job from the one described in this plan. It is worth deciding which one you want before the book forces the answer.

blocks.x: Three assumptions are worth arguing about before anything else: ten booked calls a month at steady state, a 35% proposal win rate, and 2% monthly churn. Change any of them on the Assumptions sheet and every other number in the workbook moves. Replace all three with measured figures after six discovery calls and the model stops being a guess.

blocks.title: One last time, plainly
body: Klyara has no clients and is not yet supervised. Every number in this plan is a model built on stated assumptions and real published market prices. It is not a forecast of what will happen. It is a description of what would happen if the assumptions hold — which is the only honest thing a plan for a business with no trading history can be.
